source: PB-S1#early-middle, answer to how writing with Hobert differs from ordinary conversation
song: I Love You, I'm Sorry — Gracie Abrams
finding: Abrams says writing with Audrey Hobert, a close friend, strips out the politeness of a normal session: nobody's feelings get hurt, so lines are offered and thrown out fast. Of the candidate lines, they often keep the one that makes them laugh most, and she describes the laughing as how the two of them got through big, uncomfortable adult feelings. In the voice memos, Hobert's approving 'ooh' marks a line as funny enough to keep.
quote: going with the line that makes us laugh the hardest
why_it_matters: Use laughter in the room as the test for a blunt or hurt line: if it makes the writers laugh, it usually carries the wound and the self-awareness together.
when_not: Abrams also says some lines that got a laugh sound weak on playback, and Hobert says she is not a writer who can work with just anyone (PB-S11 P9), so the test needs trust between the writers and a cold re-listen afterwards.

source: PB-S1#middle to late-middle: verse breakdown with Dessner's production; bridge discussion
song: I Love You, I'm Sorry — Gracie Abrams
finding: Abrams says she built the song in chapters across time rather than one moment. Verse one recalls an honest confession that went badly and the other person leaving. Verse two is what she calls the petty part: she watches the ex charm people at events on his own and judges him from a distance. A later section pictures them friendly years later. Most of the album's bridges rush along as manic thought, she says, but here she wanted a rhythmic change, and the bridge is where she owns her behaviour as a habit to break. She also admits a verse line hurt its subject and that she has been careless before about how people take songs written about them.
why_it_matters: Let the verses hold the past and the pettiness, and keep the bridge for the narrator's own admission, set apart by a change of rhythm rather than more speed.
when_not: Abrams' regret about hurting the subject is the cost: a petty verse works on record, but the person it is about will hear it.

source: PB-S1#late, answer to Hirway's question about the title format
song: I Love You, I'm Sorry — Gracie Abrams
finding: Abrams says the title's shape comes from an earlier song of hers, I Miss You, I'm Sorry, about the same person, and from years of drafts that used a hate version of the same formula. The formula stuck with her as a fixed point she kept coming back to. She says the feeling in the new pairing is sincere. Wikipedia also relays her telling Today (2024-07-18) that the song is a bookend to the earlier one (PB-S2).
why_it_matters: Reusing one title template across songs to the same person turns two flat clauses into an ongoing conversation, and changing the single verb shows how the relationship has moved.
when_not: The template depends on the earlier song being known; heard on its own, the title is simply two stock phrases side by side.

finding: On Song Exploder, Abrams says her voice memos come out half-mumbled, somewhere between speaking and singing, and calls this a mouth-feel thing: words are kept for how they sit in the mouth as well as for what they mean (PB-S1). In Nylon, Hobert says Abrams taught her the idea of mouthfeel, meaning checking whether words feel good strung together, and that it stayed with her. Hobert was explaining why Abrams' songs stick even when they make odd choices. She was not talking about That's So True in particular.
quote: when you see if words feel good all strung together
why_it_matters: Mumble a line before fixing its words, and judge plain conversational phrases by how they feel said one after another, not only by their sense.
when_not: Neither source gives an example of a word changed for mouthfeel, so the practice is stated rather than shown. Any judgement about how the words sound is provisional, since I worked from text only.

finding: Abrams told Nylon (Dec 2024) that she and Hobert were drunk on the roof of Electric Lady Studios when they wrote the lyric, laughing to the point of tears. She called it an angsty, sarcastic song and said the first lyrics were much nastier. Second-hand reports of a Spotify event (PB-S6, PB-S7) have her saying a far cruder version exists that will never come out. Nylon's writer, not Abrams, reads the bridge as a rushed, panicked confession. In October 2025 Abrams told People she was nervous about discussing the bridge and would not take it apart (PB-S5).
why_it_matters: Draft the jealous, unreasonable version at full ugliness for the laugh, then file it down to sarcasm: the attitude survives without the vulgarity. My inference, not Abrams' statement: a stock agreeing reply such as That's So True works as a sarcastic title once the song around it is angsty.
when_not: The evidence is thin and partly second-hand, and no source says which lines changed between the crude draft and the release.

finding: Hobert says that what she disliked in school poetry was flowery language, and that her rule for herself is to say plainly what she wants to say. She names her two goals as making people laugh and telling the truth. Her favourite line in Sue Me hangs on a real, petty detail: the clothing brand an ex always wore. W Magazine reports that the Sue Me chorus came out while she was venting to producer Ricky Gourmet and that she sang it straight away. The same piece says, in the writer's words, that she drafts lyrics like monologues and edits them for clarity and rhythm (PB-S10).
quote: My goals are to make them laugh and tell the truth
why_it_matters: A small, checkable, petty detail such as a brand or an object makes a grudge funny and believable at once, and stating it plainly beats decorating it.
when_not: Paste's critic (PB-S14, entry #11) heard Sue Me as affected diary-pop whose chorus works by brute repetition. The plain, quirky approach reads as a pose when the detail feels styled rather than lived.

finding: Young says Messy started as a bedroom demo when a relationship was ending, which gave her closure, and that she then turned to her relationship with herself. Variety's writer reports that she realised many of the lines were criticisms she aimed at herself. Elsewhere she says the addressee is a composite, largely close family as well as men (PB-S20, Capital FM relaying a TV appearance), and that the song is about looking for self-acceptance while she can be unaccepting of who she is (PB-S17). She also says she is loud and outspoken and has to own it.
quote: Then I started to think about my relationship with myself.
why_it_matters: A list of accusations that sounds aimed at a lover can come from inside the narrator's own head, and a composite addressee lets one song be a row and a self-portrait at the same time.
when_not: The interviews cover meaning, not drafting: no source shows how the swearing or the order of the lines was decided.

finding: Atwood's reviewer describes the lyric as an itemised complaint about someone who faults the narrator for opposite things and can never be satisfied, sung like an angry voicemail. The reviewer says the backing gets louder, the vocal angrier and the criticism sharper as the song goes on, and notes frequent profanity. I have not heard the track, so all claims about delivery and build are the reviewer's.
quote: as if you are watching the singer leave an angry voicemail
why_it_matters: Stack contradictory demands against the narrator so the impossibility itself becomes the hook, and raise the anger section by section instead of adding new information.
when_not: Reviewing her 2025 album, The Independent (PB-S23) notes the explicit tag on 8 of 12 tracks and says the record's strengths and weaknesses both come from its commitment to mess. Bluntness repeated across a whole album can blur.

source: PB-S29#quotes relayed from Billboard cover story; with PB-S31 and PB-S35#P13, P29
song: Girl, so confusing (version with Lorde) — Charli XCX featuring Lorde
finding: Charli says she wanted Lorde to know the song was about her before it came out, spent almost a year failing to meet her, and finally sent a voice note the day before brat's release. She says that struggle to connect mirrored the song's own story. Lorde suggested the remix herself, and Charli says it took three days in all (PB-S31). Lorde says writing her verse brought deep empathy and a sense of having been misunderstood, and that Charli's song opened a channel between them that let her say new things. Before release, Charli said brat's lyrics are what she would say privately to friends, and that being jealous is wrongly taken to mean not supporting women (PB-S35).
quote: it made me say things that I had never said
why_it_matters: An answer verse from the person the song addresses turns a petty monologue into a dialogue. Exclaim's critic (PB-S34) hears the reply working because it accepts some of the blame rather than matching the spiral.
when_not: Exclaim's critic still found Lorde's verse clumsy in places, and the format needs a real counterpart willing to answer in public. The Billboard original was blocked, so these quotes come via Complex, NME, Nylon and Stereogum, which agree with each other.

finding: On Song Exploder (2026), Charli says that on Camera she and her collaborators wanted to keep a stream-of-consciousness feel. Because the lyric is an embarrassing inner monologue, rhyme felt wrong to her: rhyme implies forethought and would make the line sound like a thought she was going back to rather than one happening now. She says a good melody is about conviction even if it stays on one note, and that a blunt line in the outro was not meant to be clever. This is a 2026 song, not from brat, and its credits are unverified.
quote: rhyme requires a bit of premeditation
why_it_matters: For interior monologue, drop or loosen the rhyme so the line sounds unplanned, and let conviction in the delivery carry it rather than melodic movement.
when_not: This is a choice for one song; she does not say rhyme is wrong for conversational pop in general, and nothing from the brat era documents the same approach.

finding: Rae says the song was called Backseat until she played it to Charli XCX, who asked why it was not called Diet Pepsi, and the title changed. Apple Music's notes say the hook was written in February 2024, on the day she met Elvira Anderfjärd and Luka Kloser (PB-S46). Wikipedia relays a Rolling Stone piece I could not open, saying the three began by humming the chorus (PB-S42). Rae says she likes trying out different deliveries of a line (PB-S45 P20).
quote: why isn't the song called Diet Pepsi?
why_it_matters: Promote the oddest concrete noun in the lyric to the title: a brand name is more specific and more sayable than a setting word like Backseat.
when_not: No source explains what the brand does in the lyric or how the words were chosen, and the claim that the melody came before the words is second-hand. Headphones On has no writer statements about its words beyond Rae calling it emotional and cathartic (relayed, PB-S43).

finding: McRae says Greedy came on the last day of a week-long session with Ryan Tedder, Amy Allen and Jasper Harris, when they chose to try something completely different, quickly and without overthinking. They built a beat and rapped ideas while sketching one scene, a man coming up to her at a bar (PB-S54). She says she first thought it was the worst song she had ever heard and found it frightening, and that Tedder pushed her for months to release it. She describes an alter ego who takes over on stage, and says many of the new songs are not how she would talk in real life.
quote: not how I would talk in real life
why_it_matters: Attitude can be written as a character the artist steps into, and one concrete scene, such as a stranger at a bar, gives the swagger something to push against.
when_not: Because the persona is not how she talks, the brash voice can feel borrowed, and McRae herself resisted it at first.

finding: McRae says the song started because Julia Michaels wanted a pop artist to recreate the Ying Yang Twins' Whisper Song, over a beat from Grant Boutin. It was her first song about sex, and she wanted it to still feel like her by keeping metaphor and story. The chorus metaphor works on two levels, so a listener could hear it as being only about a car, and she casts herself as the car on display who gets to look first. Critics, as relayed by Wikipedia (PB-S57), describe a spoken-word, whispered chorus over a stuttering beat with hip-hop influence. I have not heard it.
quote: you could literally just be thinking about a sports car
why_it_matters: A deniable object metaphor lets a first explicit song keep the artist's own voice, and the listener chooses which level to hear.
when_not: Critics mostly described it through comparisons to Britney Spears and the Pussycat Dolls, so a borrowed reference can overshadow the lyric. Revolving door, by the same team, has no writer statements about its words, and Paste (relayed, PB-S60) said its chorus builds to very little.

finding: Warren says Ordinary was written at a camp with Cal Shapiro, Mags Duval and Adam Yaron, in a house so dusty they gave it a nickname. Some lines grew out of jokes about the dust and the weak coffee there, and he finds it funny that people pick the lyrics apart, since some started as someone saying something stupid enough to be funny. Writing began after a film night with a guitar arpeggio, and the song was finished within 24 hours. He says it is about falling in love with his new wife and that he believes every word.
quote: someone says something so dumb that it's funny
why_it_matters: Grand-sounding devotional lines can start as jokes about the room; keep the joke's concrete source even when the finished line sounds solemn.
when_not: Critics (PB-S62, PB-S14) heard the same lines as stock religious and classical imagery; the joke behind a line does not come through on the record. The Variety piece shows no byline or date.

source: PB-S64#On The Bounce; Shifty Character; Out Of The Ordinary
finding: Adam Yaron, producer and co-writer, says the chorus was sketched first in voice memos and the verses were written the next morning. The three writers were still finishing the chorus lyric in the control room while he recorded guitar. He says verse one and verse two have completely different melodic structures, and the song grows slowly rather than hitting from the start. Because the chorus was not climactic enough, they raised the key by seven semitones, starting the chorus low and then jumping up an octave.
quote: The first verse doesn't match the second verse at all.
why_it_matters: When the words are plain, let structure and register do the lifting: a low chorus start followed by an octave jump gives a simple line its climax.
when_not: Yaron talks about arrangement and pitch, not word choice, so this explains why plain lines landed from the production side only.

finding: Paste's critic Casey Epstein-Gross ranked Ordinary the sixth-worst song of 2025, calling it lifeless, generic and tuned in advance to go viral, and mocking its pseudo-Christian turn. Wikipedia relays Vulture's Craig Jenkins (page blocked), who wrote that its religious and classical metaphors would not get past a high-school writing class. Against that, American Songwriter reports listeners putting it under wedding footage, pet slideshows and memorials. The same piece reports Warren's theory that a great ballad leaves you unsure whether it is about love or death.
quote: so bloodless and generic and pre-optimized
why_it_matters: Plain devotional language with no particulars travels to any occasion, which is the same quality critics call generic. Decide on purpose which one you are writing for.
when_not: The open, unspecific frame is exactly what reviewers punished: it trades critical respect for portability.

finding: Variety reports the song came out of a four-day writing camp in Palm Springs with Julian Bunetta, Ammo, Infamous and Mikky Ekko, and that Bunetta and Ekko wrote the first two verses before Swims went in to sing. Swims says the song is all about the vocal run, and asks why anyone would sing it if they cannot hit it. Variety's writer says the lyric deals with substance abuse, codependency, remorse and heartbreak, and Ekko says it drew on experiences the writers shared and felt like mind reading (PB-S70). Bunetta says he asked for a riff to show off Swims' range.
quote: With that song, it's all about the run
why_it_matters: A direct-emotion song can be built around the singer's signature move, and verses written by others for that voice can still read as confession if they come from experience the writers share.
when_not: No source discusses the wording of the chorus or why its plain phrasing works; the evidence is about vocal design, not lyric craft.
